definition: A context window is the amount of text — measured in tokens — that an AI model can consider at once. Everything the model works with in a single turn has to fit inside it: your message, the conversation so far, any documents you pasted. Once text falls outside the window, the model simply can't see it anymore.

edges.label: measured in
edges.note: Window sizes are quoted in tokens, not words or pages.

edges.label: RAG fills it wisely
edges.note: Retrieval picks the most relevant pages so the window holds signal, not noise.

edges.label: stretched with MLA
edges.note: DeepSeek's compressed attention lets more conversation fit in the same memory.

example.body: You paste 80 pages of meeting notes and ask for action items. The first half comes back perfectly. By page 60, the model starts inventing items from the early pages it can no longer see — the window overflowed. Splitting the notes into chunks, or summarizing in stages, fixes it.
example.title: The meeting notes that were too long

footnotes.body: Typical window sizes: 128K tokens (GPT-4 class), 200K (Claude), up to 1M+ on newer models. Under the hood, the model keeps a "KV cache" of everything in the window, and attention cost grows with window size — which is why huge windows cost more and run slower. Techniques like DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention compress that cache so more fits in the same memory.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: Context Window
tagline: How much text the AI can hold in its head at once — its working memory.
whyItMatters: The context window sets the ceiling on everything practical: how long a document you can paste, how long a conversation can run before the AI starts 'forgetting' the beginning, and how much background material you can feed it. When the AI seems to lose track of earlier details, this is almost always why.
